Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Okay.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Now, there is an instance in which men will go to a village and deliberately take a woman, but it's only when woman has run away from a cruel husband in her village and flees to another village. She better be sure that that village she flees to has a lot of tough guys in it, because she's almost certain to be pursued and recaptured by her ex-husband and his brothers, and then she'll be severely punished for doing that.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: So presumably the women you're talking about are those in their late teens, or could be they be older, up to their late thirties?

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Yes. They would have a better chance of being taken into the other village the younger they are.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Do men ever marry older women?

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Oh, yes.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Why would that be?

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Can't find one that's suitable, and more attractive. They'll marry anybody. You can't really classify the Yanomamo as monogamous, polygamous, and polyandrous. Nor do I suspect you can do that with any society, or at least societies of the sort that you're interested in, like hunters and gatherers, transisting from hunting and gathering, to agriculture; or early agricultural societies like the Yanomamo. You have to look at marriage as a life history event. So when you're young and don't have a lot of kinsmen, the best game in town might be sharing a wife with your brother. So at that point your marriage is polyandrous. Then as you age, or your kinship fortunes increase--like more of your own kinsmen move to your village--then you might be able to do a wife all by yourself. And then if you become politically important and have a lot of relatives and lots of sisters to give away in marriage, you might end up with two or three wives. The most wives a Yanomamo I know has ever had is six at the same time. One of the papers I'm going to do is how many spouses each sex has throughout their lifetime; just to try to add some dimension to this argument about polygamy, polyandry, and monogamy.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: So when you say spouse, what do you mean by that? What is spouse, just somebody you're sleeping in the same hut with?

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: No. They formally acknowledge marriage.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: They formally acknowledge.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Yes. Like, if you ask them who's married to whom, they'll tell you.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Okay.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: But the verb they use is "bou." That means to possess. "Who does such-and-such a guy possess?" He'll say the name of his wife.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: How would they say who is she married to, you know ..

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: They would say, "Who owns her?"

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Who owns her?

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: But it's not really ownership. To possess implies something more broad and has certain dimensions and responsibilities involved there.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Is it the same word as who owns this sack of beans or this ...

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: No, it's not. It could be used that way. But when it comes to people, you know, that they're talking about being married, or having a spouse.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: They have a separate word.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: So how many marriages are from within the village and how many from somebody coming in from the outside?

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: It depends on the size of your village. It's a huge numbers game.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Okay.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Big villages lord over small villages. So if you're seeking an ally who will protect you from the people up the hill who are bigger than you, you're at a disadvantage because in order to get allies, you've got to give women to them. It's an economics game where the smaller village has to pay up front for the privileges of the alliance, and the bigger village tends to default on many of its agreements. So big villages tend to exploit small villages. It's always a good idea to live in a big village; however, it's like living in a powder keg.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Why does it matter militarily whether you're in a big village or a small village, given that the raids are surprise attacks?

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Because it depresses the enthusiasm of your neighbors to sneak attack you, because you way outnumber them.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Because there's the possibility that a really large attack will be made in return.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Yes. And since there are so many people they can get around you and intercept you on the retreat.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: So what's the largest number of raiders you ever saw?

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Probably 70, 75. The smallest is ten.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Oh. I thought raiding parties were smaller than that. You always get a pretty good posse before you go do anything.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: If a village can't field 10 raiders, that pretty much determines the minimum size of the village. If it's not large enough, and demographically structured in a certain way to produce ten able-bodied men to go on raids, it's likely it may not a viable village.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: But if the point of the raid is honor.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: It's revenge.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: It's an honor or revenge thing, so that they'd go to punish that village by killing one of their men or ...

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: It's not to be confused with the Mediterranean sense of honor.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Okay.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: It's to get revenge because they killed my brother.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Okay.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: And they didn't deflower my little sister. And that's honor.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Now, all this basically political lore that you've just been telling us the last five minutes, do you hear the kids talking about this?

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: No. Well, they might talk about it, but I didn't do my study on children.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: So for one reason or another, talking to the kids was not an activity that you could comfortably engage in?

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: No. Well, I could comfortably engage in it, but I didn't want to waste my time. I talked to the adults. Those are the decision makers. The kids do not decide who's going to go on a raid.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: But it might be really interesting.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: But I only have one life to lead.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Okay. Fair enough.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Every time I get in a conversation with experts in any particular field, they frequently ask, "why didn't you study this?" Well ...

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: I'm still a little unable to imagine why your hosts in the villages you were in didn't kill you. They didn't kill you because that's killing the golden goose and you had ...

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: In some villages.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: And you had the medicine, and the fishhooks, and all that. But why didn't they just say, "Give us all your fishhooks and medicine right now?" Why didn't the strongman just take everything?

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Well, that's why I stopped studying this one village.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Because they did?

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Yes. He wanted to. He wanted my shotgun at the end. People in the Yanomamo villages in Brazil--the missionaries give them guns, and he wanted my shotgun. "When you leave, just leave your gun behind." No. And I knew that so long as he remained in that village I would never go back, either because he'd kill me or I'd kill him in self-defense. And it's not good to kill your informants.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: That's true.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: The American Anthropological Association has policies about that.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Okay. So here's the last question.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: It better be a big one.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: It is. As you know, a few decades ago Elizabeth and I lived with the Lese farmers of the north-eastern Congo for nine months. After several months of being there, Elizabeth, who grew up in a small village in England, said, "You know, exotic as all this behavior is, basically, it all feels incredibly familiar." Did you feel that life among the Yanamamo was basically familiar from the sense of the relationships that you witnessed growing up?

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: Yes. The villages that I became really involved in, like Bisaasi-teri and these were just like my good friends, and even some of my relatives, and it was not like observer-observed kind of relationship. I wept at their funerals, and things like that. They played with my kids in the short time my kids were there. So it's very easy to empathize and recognize, even as an anthropologist or maybe a missionary, how similar these people are to you. They may have exotic customs, and eat grubs an inch long, but basically, when you scratch them, they bleed red and have emotions like yours. Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: UNITING THE CULTURAL AND BIOLOGICAL DIMENSIONS OF MAN'S EXISTENCE IN A TOUGH AND EXACT SCIENTIFIC FRAMEWORK This began as an exhilarating exercise celebrating the verve and intelligence of a colleague and friend who has made serious contribution to understanding human beings. However it unexpectedly veered to a mood of rue and woe about the stolid incompetence of countless disciplineless scholars as they survey the human condition. Why this sudden shift? In preparing to write the comment Edge has invited I thought to go back to one consequential source of the creation of this whole business and reviewed the recommendations Robin Fox and I made to the Guggenheim Foundation about Napoleon's project. Let me note first that Harry Guggenheim left a legacy of dollars to study what he very innovatively perceived as the pan-human sources of aggression and inequality. Fox and I were asked to be co-Research Directors of the program and I will take the liberty of recalling what we advised our Board of Directors about Nap's work in the context of the ambient anthropology of the time. I do this with pride because we were apparently so prescient and clear about the gallant work, but also with great dyspepsia about the fact that we wrote on this matter 39 years ago and what has changed? The responses to the situation such as by Marshall Sahlins five minutes ago and others occurred yesterday and today and given modern universities which segregate natural from social science will tomorrow too. Social behavior cannot of course be natural. Everyone knows that. How atmospherically depressing. On April 1 1974 (four decades ago Comrades) Fox and I wrote "We have been concerned always to look for projects that unite the cultural and biological dimensions of man's existence....It is extremely rare to find a project which combines these approaches in a tough and exact scientific framework. Dr Chagnon is one of the outstanding younger American anthropologists and an investigator trained in both the study of social structure and in genetics and population biology. Here we have in the Yanomamo documentation with a degree of exactness and scientific objectivity that is not open to challenge. What Chagnon has discovered is a population in which essentially warfare plays a role not only in establishing social but genetic dominance where the most successful warriors have the most wives and offspring and where the most war-like populations expand at the expense of their neighbors. We have somewhat increased Chagnon's original budget since we felt he was underestimating the expenses he would need to carry out the project". In response to Nap's request for a continuation we noted that "What we have here is...an ideal opportunity to test the relative merits of a multi-dimensional approach vs. the rather simple-minded ecological deterministic approach". Chagnon lived through the tumult of his time in the spotlight. Too many of us shared that trial by inaccurate fire. I had made the mistake in 1969 of examining sex differences at the moment of noisy incarnation of a post-modernist feminist movement that saw sex roles mainly as the result of reading this or that magazine and detested biology. I had bomb threats at a lecture at McGill, predictions of broken knees at a New School graduate seminar, endured a television riot on David Frost's first network show in the US and when Robin and I spoke at a BBC event about The Imperial Animal filmed at the Royal Society in London a noisy group of Trotskyite men dressed as English ladies with flower hats (don't ask) dramatically swept out of the amphitheatre after 20 minutes. Napoleon's travail along with Wilson's and many others was testament to the glandular ferocity of opponents rooted in the stew of self-righteous antipathies they called culture And of course they despised nature, unless it featured acid rain and other environmental insults. That the contest continues with such avidity is appalling tribute to the comfortable durability of a system of ideas untrammeled by intellectual boots on the ground except for those near the used copies of Foucault in bookstores in choicest Paris. Sunnis and Shia share cultural enjoyment of ebbing blood of dying enemies. Why? Serbs raped to impregnate enemy women and imprisoned them until abortions were impossible. Nazis had farms for blue-eyed  babies. These were errors of planning of Chagnon and the likes of him and us? Why is there such unstinting avidity for environmental nature but so little for inner-environmental human nature?

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
Name: [Redacted]
Text: COMMENT ON EDGE EVENT: "NAPOLEON CHAGNON: BLOOD IS THEIR ARGUMENT" Probably no single phrase cost Napoleon Chagnon more enemies than when he wrote that the Yanomamo live << in a state of chronic warfare >>. More than four decades on, the evidence that many human societies without a state have lived with high levels of violence over long periods is now very strong (a paper by Samuel Bowles in Science in 2009 reviews that evidence). This evidence is compatible with there being much lower levels of violence in other circumstances, in different societies as well as in the same societies at other times. Indeed, the implication is that levels of violence are capable of changing quite fast over time--which suggests an important role for cultural influences. This makes it all the more surprising that a belief that at least some societies without a state might be or have been very violent has come to be widely associated with biological determinism, the idea that our biology predestines us to a violent life. Why has this happened, when the association of the two ideas is so contrary to basic logic? One part of the explanation must lie in the hypothesis that natural selection might have rewarded males who indulged a taste for violence, by giving them greater access to females and therefore larger numbers of surviving offspring. Chagnon's evidence that this was true for Yanomamo males has aroused enormous controversy. Interestingly, a study by Clayton and Carole Robarchek of the Waorani of Ecuador, which prior to peaceful contact had known spectacular levels of violence, examined data similar to that of Chagnon's, noting that "at first glance the data were markedly similar to those presented by Chagnon, and they certainly seemed to support the sociobiological hypothesis". The Robarcheks, noting that "we were uneasy", went on to propose an alternative interpretation of the data. This illustrates, however, that the original Chagnon interpretation was far from outrageous, and while other scholars are free to disagree with it there seems no scientific basis for the hostility that it aroused. The hostility seems best to be explained by the belief that if natural selection had created some tendency among males to indulge a taste for violence under some conditions, this must render violence inevitable or undermine attempts to sanction it morally. But this conclusion is just false. Human beings are spectacularly adaptable animals, able to modify our behavior across a very wide range of environmental conditions. Many humans, more often males than females though not exclusively so, can be highly violent when circumstances encourage their doing so with impunity. The same individuals can behave highly peacefully when circumstances encourage that instead. It is just false to think that this must be less likely under Chagnon's hypothesis than if, say, violence were driven entirely by the desire to acquire physical property, which has for a long time been the favored alternative. Given how risky violence is to those who engage in it, trying to understand why they do so is an entirely legitimate scientific aim. It is, moreover, an essential precondition for devising policies that can reduce violence in our own societies. Ruling out particular hypotheses in advance (such as the hypothesis that violence has been associated with a sexual reward, and that it may therefore flourish more easily in circumstances that evoke to the participants the possibility of such a sexual reward), is not just bad science; it's also bad policy-making. At the moment it seems to me that the jury is still out on whether such a hypothesis is supported by the evidence, and if so how important a phenomenon that is. But it is disturbing to see how much hostility can be directed at researchers for merely considering it. For much of the twentieth century there was a dominant view of hunter-gatherer societies that claimed they were largely egalitarian and largely peaceful, until agriculture and sedentarism arrived to disturb the primordial harmony. Much new evidence has come in, and interestingly, that view has not been entirely discredited--only partially so. The evidence that hunter-gatherer societies were fairly egalitarian has held up rather well against such evidence. But the nature of that egalitarianism now looks very different from the view (dating back to Jean-Jacques Rousseau) that human beings have no natural tendencies towards competitiveness and hierarchy. Instead, it seems much more likely that such tendencies were counter-balanced in hunter-gatherer societies by a willingness of individuals to cooperate against any of their number who sought to abuse and profit from lording it over others (as argued in Christopher Boehm's book Hierarchy in the Forest). On the question of violence, however, the twentieth century view now looks much wider of the mark. It might have been otherwise, but it now no longer looks that way. Even if there were grounds for thinking that greater violence in our past implies that we should be pessimistic about the possibility of eradicating violence in our present, it would not be a reason for distorting our scientific methods. But what is really mystifying is why that inference, from violence in our past to pessimism about our present, should ever have become part of the conventional wisdom in the first place.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument

Text: WELCOME TO THE JUNGLE: ANARCHY FROM THE AMAZON TO THE ATOMIC AGE "Force is a means of achieving the external ends of states because there exists no consistent, reliable process of reconciling the conflicts of interest that inevitably arise among similar units in a condition of anarchy." This was Kenneth Waltz, one of the fathers of international relations, writing about the behavior of nation-states in the international system. But it could just as well have been written about the Yanomamo, the "fierce people" of the Amazon. As legendary anthropologist Napoleon Chagnon notes, every village lives under the shadow of its vulnerability to attack from other villages, "Even the missionaries who have lived among the Yanomano the longest have pointed out repeatedly to me and other people that these people are terrified of neighbors. It's like Hobbes's war of 'all against all'". Comparing small-scale indigenous societies to modern nation-states is a hazardous exercise, because so many things are obviously different. However, what is perhaps even more striking is that some things remain remarkably similar. Here I consider three aspects common to the Amazon jungle and the jungle of international politics: Anarchy, alliances, and war. Anarchy Within states, there are rules, which can be governed and enforced. But between states, rules are absent or weak, and unenforceable. The result: Anarchy. Anarchy does not mean that all hell is constantly breaking loose. But the effects are no less significant. Anarchy means that states do not have an overarching level of governance, no "Leviathan" in Hobbes' words, to protect them. States must fend for themselves. And in fending for themselves, the only reliable means available is to maximize their power. While the Yanomamo might be in a Hobbesian state of nature, at the pinnacle of civilization today we find ourselves facing exactly the same problem, just at a monumental scale. As in the Yanomano, "Big villages lord over small villages." Or as Kenneth Waltz would put it, international politics is about power. Alliances There is, however, a saving grace in anarchy, which is also strikingly fundamental to both the Yanomano and international politics: Alliances. While a state is condemned to a given size and geographic location, it can instantly double, triple, or even further increase its deterrent or military power by the simple expedient of finding an ally. Whenever there are mutual benefits, usually mutual enemies, the intense collective action problem under anarchy can be solved. The First World war was a conflict not between countries but between powerful alliances--the Triple Entente of Britain, France, and Russia and the Central Powers of Germany, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire. The Second World War was a clash of the Allies against the Axis Powers. Even in times of peace, alliances are vital. The Cold War was an intense struggle of deterrence between NATO and the Warsaw Pact. Alliances are a regularly recurring pattern of history, stretching back to Thucydides history of the 5th century BC Peloponnesian war between the allies of Athens and the allies of Sparta, and through the wars of history ever since. From Chagnon's work, we know that alliances were vital and decisive there too. Villages will ally with each other to improve their deterrence, or to mount raids on other villages. Any one village is restricted in size, but joining with another village can instantly double its size and double it power. Alliances to maintain the balance of power have likely been the handmaiden of human evolution as well as of history. War and Peace But most states, and Yanomamo villages, most of the time, are at peace. So why is war so important? What matters is not war itself, but the threat of war. Chagnon makes clear in his work that, while the Yanomamo do not fight all the time, life is pervaded by the fear of your neighbors. If a raid only happens once a year, you may fear it every day. This is important because humans have always organized their societies not around war, but around the possibility of war. Nations spend a hefty fraction of their GDP preparing for wars that, usually, do not happen. The United States spends hundreds of billions of dollars a year on defense (and offense) whether it is at war or not. Switzerland has compulsory military service and a multi-million man reserve army, but has not fought a war for 500 hundred years. A Martian anthropologist collecting data on the incidence of war during the last half-century might well have concluded that the US and USSR were good friends. States may not be at war, but they are constantly on a war footing, exercising strategies to deter potential enemies, forging alliances, training standing armies, and developing new weapons. To a large extent, international politics is about war whether it is occurring or not. From Chagnon's work, we can see that this phenomenon may be at play in our ancestral roots as well as today. The Yanomamo organize their villages and social structure with war in mind. As Chagnon notes, "life was very much filled with terror of your neighbors". Groups that cannot field around 10 able-bodied men, he found, may not be a viable village because this is a minimum size to deter enemies, bargain with allies, and be able to fight. In terms of wars' effect on human nature, there is also the criterion of natural selection, which cares not about the incidence of war but its impact on reproduction. Even if war is rare, humans live long. While the majority of Yanomamo may survive a given raid, they may live to die another day. The probability of death from war over, say, a 40-year period at some point in the lives of warring peoples is hardly insignificant in the eyes of evolution. Rare events can still leave scars on our DNA. Human Nature and Human Organization So far we have seen striking parallels between the Yanomamo and international politics, not least in the problem of anarchy, the importance of alliances, and the effects of war on life during peace. There are clearly two issues surfacing here: (1) human nature; and (2) human organization. As Kenneth Waltz noted in his classic Man, The State and War, "States in the world are like individuals in the state of nature. They are neither perfectly good nor are they controlled by law." In other words, in both cases--states and individuals--we need an understanding of the anarchic environment in which people find themselves, as well as an understanding of their natural dispositions in how they respond. And it is here that the Yanomamo and international politics diverge radically, but with insights from the former still flowing to enlighten the latter. While there may be remarkable similarities between conflict between small-scale societies and states in international politics, there are also significant differences, most notably in scale, weapons, and levels of organization. Human judgment and decision-making mechanisms evolved to deal with the challenges of our evolutionary past, not those of today. And the modern phenomenon of large, settled, agricultural societies has sprung up in the last 10,000 years, in a change far too rapid for our fundamental cognitive machinery to have evolved along with it. Therefore, we often face the problem of "evolutionary mismatch": human behaviors that were adaptive in our evolutionary past but which are maladaptive in our modern environment. Our emotions, for example, may bring us time in jail rather than offspring in the jungle. As similar as the problem of anarchy may be in small-scale societies and modern international politics, human beings may find themselves better equipped to deal with the former than the latter. As we know, history is littered with as many examples of misjudgment and recklessness as it is with wisdom and foresight, and this is in part due--as many political scientists would attest--to a range of evolved biases in cognition, motivation, emotion, information processing, decision-making, learning, and memory. As Waltz recognized, humans are not "perfectly good." What evolutionary anthropology offers is the chance to explore and understand these dispositions and biases, and armed with our growing biological knowledge of human nature--thanks to the hard work of people like Napoleon Chagnon--we will be in a better position to understand, predict, and perhaps improve human behavior. The War at Home Napoleon Chagnon has done humanity a great service in rescuing a rare window onto our evolutionary past. As the so-called Anthropocene has surged forward, we have gradually wiped out the opportunity to observe human beings in our "the state of nature". Until we invent a time machine, the opportunity is about to close forever. Without information like that courageously and carefully collected by Chagnon, we would only ever be guessing what humans might have been like before agriculture, technology, and mass societies have covered up our tracks for good. So why all the controversy? When I first read Chagnon's work it all made perfect sense. Having been trained as a biologist, the idea that biology might have something to do with explaining a biological organism like human beings was not an unreasonable proposition. As I think was obvious to most scientists, it might not be the whole explanation, but without it our understanding would be significantly hobbled. As a result, I could never make head or tail of the intensity of flak that Chagnon and other evolutionary anthropologists were attracting--that understanding would have to wait until I spent more time among my new tribe of humanist and social scientists. But in any case I was undeterred by whatever flak there might be, because science offered a way to move forward and resolve the conflict. Evolutionary biology, like any other science, generates predictions derived from theory, for which you can go out, collect data, and test them. We are not limited to argument and criticism, as many social science disciplines are. We can test rival explanations with empirical information and see which ones are better able to explain variation in the data. Of course, people will always debate methods and measurements and interpretations of data, but there is a steady progress, not stasis or regression. From my experience living among the "enemy", crossing the lines from biology to social science, it has become clear that resistance is not due to social scientists not knowing about evolution, or having studied and examined the arguments and rejected it on intellectual grounds, it is rather that they are ideologically opposed to it. The philosophical traditions in many social science fields have created a taboo which says that biology does not, cannot, and must not matter. Like the injured Yanomamo warrior in Chagnon's account, who could not drink water when he most needed it, taboos can sometimes lead to disaster. In our case, of what I see as a fear of knowledge, this has gone so far as for people to have put an ideological opposition to scientific inquiry into a written declaration in the Seville Statement on Violence, adopted by UNESCO in 1989. It declares, among other finger wagging statements, that "It is scientifically incorrect to say that in the course of human evolution there has been a selection for aggressive behaviour more than for other kinds of behaviour." Some of the Seville Statements points are reasonable cautions, but the overall mission of making ideological pre-commitments instead of, or in the active prevention of, examining evidence is a return to pre-Enlightenment thinking. What I find telling is that in the constantly resurfacing of the nature versus nuture debate, no biologist on Earth will tell you that human behavior is 100% nature and 0% nuture. That would simply be a misunderstanding of biology. Genetic dispositions are important but only part of the story. Yet, it is quite easy to find people--even many learned scholars--who will tell you that human behavior is 100% nuture and 0% nature. There is a striking asymmetry of open-mindedness here: biologists take the middle ground, which is based on data; opponents take an extreme position, which is often based on no data at all. It appears that the arrival of the new synthesis in biology is somewhat akin to the arrival of Napoleon Chagnon in a new Yanomamo village. Along with the fascination of a novel stranger, there was a sometimes a strong impulse that he should be killed.` At noted above, I started out optimistic because evolutionary approaches generate hypotheses that can be tested with data and compared to alternative hypotheses--and then accepted, rejected, or revised. However, a good deal of pessimism must remain, because so much of social science is beautifully literate in language, but amazingly illiterate in scientific methods, statistics, and data. In our scientific age, understanding data should be as important as reading and writing. Until modern society improves its standards of scientific literacy, theories and approaches based on data may remain irrelevant for the large audiences that cannot read them--especially those ideologically opposed to their ideas or methods in the first place. For them, reading them or learning the language would be pointless. Similar problems can be seen in my own field of political science. The grim view of anarchy laid out above is generally referred to as realism. There are other views as well, of course. All of them accept the underlying problem of anarchy, even if only to examine how it is perceived or circumvented. "Neoliberals" agree on the problem of anarchy but are optimistic that it can be overcome by trade (making war too expensive), democracy (since democratic nations have never, so far, fought each other), and international institutions (creating a Leviathan after all). At the other end of the spectrum, "constructivists" point to the fact that humans can create their own reality and, to put it simply, if we see conflict and threats we will fear and fight them. "Anarchy is what states make of it", as Alexander Wendt famously opined. Constructivists point instead to the role of ideas and norms, and the individuals who can transform these ideals and norms into policy and practice. But for all of these theoretical approaches, there is plenty of room, indeed a vast chasm, for the injection of biological theory. Even among modern realists, who might recognize Yanomamo life as remarkably similar to their own anthropological subjects, nation-states, the problem of war is a problem of the structure of the international system of states--it is a problem of anarchy, not a problem of human nature. Indeed, it was precisely the perceived problems of getting from human nature to the behavior of nation-states that had led them away from the "classical" realism of Hobbes to Waltz's "neorealism". But the more we know about human nature, the better we can understand how humans respond, conflict, and cooperate under the crippling conditions of anarchy. War plays a central role in this understanding. It was the quest to understand the causes of war gave rise to the whole academic field of international relations in the first place, as the world reeled to explain and avert the horrors of the First World War. The causes of war remains a central area of study in the discipline today--with, it should be added, very little consensus. Like anthropologists' divergent views over the incidence and impact of war among indigenous societies, international relations scholars cannot agree on even basic things such as whether nuclear weapons are a force for peace or war, whether states are primarily interested in relative or absolute gains, whether war is costly or beneficial, or whether great power war is really in decline or merely in remission. But amidst all of this confusion, remarkably, the idea that war might have something to do with human beings is not only nowhere to be seen, but the mere idea is widely opposed. When people raise the possibility, it is often received in abject horror. Like the anthropologists that were offended by Napoleon Chagnon's findings on the Yanomamo, political scientists are similarly resistant to evolutionary insights for human behavior. It is as though we are happy to study cars in our quest to understand the phenomenon of traffic, but we are unwilling to lift the hood to confront the complex engine whirring underneath. For one thing, we might get our hands dirty. But things are changing. Its not so much that Napoleon Chagnon won the argument. Rather, he was on the right side of history, and history is catching up with him. But that is no accident, given that he was one of its pioneers. He and a growing army of evolutionary scientists have launched us on a new journey of discovery, and one that is already yielding significant fruit in what some are calling the Age of Biology. The 0% nature view is going to have an increasingly tough time as our knowledge of genetics, neuroscience, experimental psychology, and evolutionary psychology advances ever more rapidly. The question really is why such a relatively small number of critics of Napoleon Chagnon, and people endowed with a similar vision, have been so vocal. Perhaps it is because they're swimming against the tide, and they're vocal because they are drowning. I, for one, am looking ahead for the promise of new shores.

Title: Napoleon Chagnon: Blood Is Their Argument
